newsitem.title: PERU: More Peru hostages to be freed, rebel leader says.
newsitem.headline: More Peru hostages to be freed, rebel leader says.

text.p: Marxist rebel leader Nestor Cerpa, in a dramatic walkie-talkie contact, promised on Saturday to carry on gradually freeing captives in Peru's hostage crisis who were not connected to the government.
Speaking via two-way radio from the besieged residence live with Peru's Channel Four television, Cerpa said the fate of officials held hostage would depend on the response of the government.

"The majority (of the hostages) who are not tied to the politics of the government we are going to free gradually and (for) those who are connected to government functions everything will depend on the will of the government," Cerpa said. He did not give any date.
Police identified Cerpa as the leader of the estimated 20 heavily armed rebels who occupied the residence last Tuesday and seized a glittering array of hostages.
The communication between the rebels and the TV station was established after the rebels held a notice up to a window telling the channel to seek them on a certain radio frequency.
Cerpa's words threw doubt on the authenticity of an earlier phone call to a radio station saying absolutely all the captives would be freed at 10 pm on December 24.

Authorities have not been able to confirm that the phone call was genuine and the rebels themselves held up a notice at a residence window after reports of the call to say their phone lines had been cut.

Cerpa's walkie-talkie remarks were followed shortly afterwards by words from men who identified themselves as the captive Peruvian Foreign Minister, Francisco Tudela, and the Japanese ambassador, Morihishi Aoki.
Journalists who knew Tudela said the voice on the radio sounded like his.

Tudela said he was being well treated by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels and urged President Alberto Fujimori's government to establish a channel of communication with the guerrillas to negotiate a solution.
He said he believed the MRTA was willing to reach a peaceful end to the crisis through negotiation but cautioned that the guerrillas were well-trained and well-armed.
Aoki, sounding nervous and speaking in broken Spanish, also said it was essential that the government and the MRTA negotiate.
